about.title: City of Industry Slip & Fall Claims
about.longDescription: City of Industry runs on commerce — sprawling logistics centers, big-box retail, and loading yards line corridors like Valley Boulevard, Gale Avenue, and Azusa Avenue. That volume of foot and forklift traffic means spills, uneven pallets, cracked pavement, and poorly lit stairwells are common culprits behind falls here. Under California law, a property owner or business isn't automatically liable just because someone fell on their premises — you generally need to show they knew, or reasonably should have known, about the hazard and didn't fix it or warn you. That's why quick action matters: photos of the hazard, incident reports, and surveillance footage (which many businesses recycle within days) can make or break a claim. LawProactive doesn't practice law — we're a free service that connects injured people in City of Industry with an independent personal injury attorney who can evaluate what happened and help you understand your options, working on contingency so there's no upfront cost.

items.title: Notice Is the Whole Case
items.desc: California requires showing the property owner knew or should have known about the hazard. An attorney can help gather maintenance logs, prior complaints, and inspection records to establish that notice.

items.title: Video Disappears Fast
items.desc: Many City of Industry warehouses and retail stores overwrite surveillance footage within days or weeks. Getting a preservation letter out quickly can be the difference between having evidence and losing it.

items.title: Comparative Fault Won't Erase Your Claim
items.desc: California is a pure comparative fault state, so even if you're found partly responsible for the fall, you may still recover a reduced amount. An attorney can help present the facts fairly instead of letting an insurer overstate your share of blame.

items.question: I slipped in a warehouse-district parking lot near Gale Avenue. Do I have a case?
items.answer: It depends on whether the property owner or manager knew, or should have known, about the hazard — like a pothole, oil spill, or poor lighting — and failed to address it. An independent attorney can look at photos, witness statements, and the property's maintenance history to assess whether that notice requirement is met. Every situation is different, so a free case review is the best next step.

items.question: How long do I have to file a slip and fall claim in California?
items.answer: Generally you have two years from the date of the fall to file a lawsuit, but if a government-owned property is involved — say, a public sidewalk or municipal building — the deadline to act is much shorter and involves a separate claims process. Missing these deadlines can end your ability to recover anything, so it's worth getting guidance early.

items.question: The store said they have no video of my fall — now what?
items.answer: That happens more often than people expect, especially with businesses that automatically delete footage after a set number of days. An attorney can send a formal preservation request quickly and may still be able to build your case using incident reports, employee statements, or physical evidence at the scene. Acting fast is the key factor here.
